newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's colonial masters sail into the sunset.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's colonial masters sail into the sunset.

text.p: The luxury liner Queen Elizabeth 2 sailed gracefully into the sunset on Saturday carrying a handful of British mandarins retiring ahead of the handover of the British colony to China later this year.
Tears and champagne flowed as the departing Britons bade farewell to their lives as members of Her Majesty's Overseas Civil Service.
They leave behind them the comforts of servants, subsidised housing and a lifestyle that, from the perspective of their desk-bound counterparts in London, was distinctly exotic.
But colonial civil servants are rapidly becoming an endangered species as Hong Kong prepares for the end of more than 150 years of British rule.

So is the perk of a cruise home which dates back to the days before air transport and allows civil servants aged over 50 or with 15 years service in hand to sail home at the Hong Kong taxpayer's expense.
The benefit was dropped from new contracts in 1984 after Hong Kong's legislators objected to the cost -- about HK$60,000 ($7,700) a head.
Hong Kong will have to foot the bill for the 270 officials and more than 90 family members who chose to exercise their privilege this year.
Last year, about 30 civil servants sailed away.
There has been an exodus of British officers and police as the handover at midnight on June 30 looms.
Some found their jobs "localised" and were forced to leave. Others were reluctant to serve under the Chinese flag or unwilling to accept demotion.
Hong Kong's new constitution, which takes effect on July 1, prohibits non-Chinese from occupying the top posts in the 180,000-strong bureaucracy.
"My children are grown up and I'm unlikely to find a new job at my age. Besides I love it here," said a British police officer who had earlier bade farewell to departing colleagues.
"But younger men have to think about the longer term."
But for those who had to go, this was the way to do it.

Cushioned by generous pensions paid to those forced to retire, the 16 civil servants and their families on the Queen Elizabeth 2 went out in style, gliding past the glass and marble skyscrapers lining one of the world's most spectacular harbours as night fell.
Their journey to a home many left decades ago will be a leisurely one, giving them plenty of opportunity to wind down from the frenzy of Hong Kong life.
The month-long voyage takes in Bangkok, Dubai and the Mediterranean before the ship docks back in Britain.
More than 50 civil servants sailed out on the opulent cruise ship Oriana on Thursday.
The Oriana is due to call at Sabah, Singapore, Mauritius, South Africa, Namibia, Cape Verde and Tenerife before arriving back in Britain.
